passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of two novel cognitive enhancers on reaction time in a controlled laboratory setting. Ninety healthy adults were randomly assigned to one of three groups: a control group receiving a placebo, Treatment A receiving drug X, and Treatment B receiving drug Y. Each participant completed a standardized computer-based reaction time task consisting of 60 trials. The mean reaction times (in milliseconds) and standard deviations were recorded, along with the sample size for each group. The results are summarized in Table 1 below. The data suggest that both treatments reduced reaction times relative to the control, with Treatment B showing the largest reduction. However, the variability in responses differed across groups. Researchers plan to conduct a follow-up study to assess long‑term effects and potential side effects. The current findings provide preliminary evidence that drug Y may be more effective at improving cognitive speed, but further investigation is needed to confirm these results and determine clinical relevance.
table_data:
Table 1: Mean reaction times (ms) and standard deviations for each group
| Group | Mean RT (ms) | SD (ms) | N |
| Control | 350 | 20 | 30 |
| Treatment A | 320 | 25 | 30 |
| Treatment B | 310 | 22 | 30 |
stem: Which of the following best describes the pattern of reaction times across groups?
explanation: The table shows mean reaction times of 350 ms (control), 320 ms (Treatment A), and 310 ms (Treatment B). Thus the order from highest to lowest is Control > Treatment A > Treatment B.
trap: Choosing a reversed ordering (Control < A < B) by treating lower reaction times as larger values.

stem: Which feature of the study design best supports attributing the lower reaction times to the drugs rather than to preexisting differences between groups?

options.A: Random assignment of participants to the three groups
options.B: Use of a computer-based reaction time task
options.D: Reporting the SD of each group

explanation: Correct: Random assignment tends to balance participant characteristics across groups, so differences in outcome are more likely due to treatment. Why the others are wrong: B) a computer-based task standardizes measurement but does not balance the groups. C) more trials per person improves measurement precision, not group comparability. D) reporting SDs describes variability and does not control confounding.
trap: Choosing a measurement feature (the standardized task or number of trials) that improves precision but does not address group comparability.

stem: Which of the following conclusions is NOT supported by Table 1 alone?

options.A: Both treatment groups had lower mean reaction times than the control group.
options.B: Treatment B had the lowest mean reaction time.
options.C: Treatment B is significantly more effective than Treatment A.
options.D: Treatment A had the greatest variability in reaction times.

explanation: Table 1 reports only means and SDs, with no inferential test. The 10 ms difference between B (310) and A (320) is small relative to SDs of 22 to 25 ms (d about 0.4), so "significantly more effective" is not supported. The other statements follow directly from the table (SDs: control 20, A 25, B 22).
trap: A lower mean does not by itself establish a statistically significant difference.

stem: What is the percent reduction in mean reaction time for Treatment B relative to the control group?
explanation: Correct: (350 - 310)/350 × 100 = 11.4%. Why the others are wrong: B) 12.9% divides the 40 ms difference by the Treatment B mean (310) instead of the control mean. C) 8.6% is the reduction for Treatment A (30/350). D) 40% is the raw difference in ms, not a percent.
trap: Dividing the 40 ms difference by the treated-group mean (310 ms) rather than the control baseline (350 ms), giving 12.9%.
